title: Implementing Network-level QoS at HPC Datacenters to Enable Distributed Scientific Workflows
problem: HPC datacenters must simultaneously handle real-time streams (sub-millisecond latency) and bulk transfers (multi-gigabit throughput), but these objectives inherently compete on shared networks, creating performance variability.
motivation: Network 'last-mile' in HPC datacenters remains best-effort, creating latency and jitter accumulation that jeopardizes time-sensitive workflows. Wide-area networks (ESnet) already implement QoS, but local ingress remains unmanaged.
method: Packets are labeled at the source computer with priority markers (DSCP—Differentiated Services Code Point, a standard way to identify traffic type) that indicate whether they carry real-time streams or bulk data. Existing network switches read these labels and queue packets separately by priority class. At the edge gateway to the high-speed network, the system controls how fast each priority class of packets can be transmitted—real-time traffic goes through immediately while bulk transfers are rate-limited.
key_novelty: This is the first deployment of DSCP-based traffic prioritization in an HPC datacenter's local network, achieving performance guarantees without requiring new hardware or custom software.
contributions: DSCP-based QoS solution on existing leaf-spine Ethernet infrastructure
Host-based packet marking with per-class queuing
Last-mile hop shaping through HSN gateway NIC
Deployable on operational fabrics without hardware changes
limitations: DSCP compliance not guaranteed across all network equipment; WAN coordination required; effectiveness depends on proper traffic classification at ingress.
